3	## Setting
4	
5	You are building the policy management system for the **Most Honorable
6	Privileged Claims Office for Magical Risks and Cursed Items** (MHPCO),
7	an old-fashioned insurance institution that covers magical items —
8	swords, amulets, staves, potions, and components such as runes and
9	moonstones. The MHPCO is bureaucratic, slightly stingy, and proud of
10	its venerable traditions.
11	
12	## Feature
13	
14	The system supports two operations: **quote** computes the premium for
15	a list of items a customer wishes to insure, and **claim** processes a
16	damage report against an existing policy.
17	
18	## Rules
19	
20	### Item values and base premiums
21	
22	Each main item has an insurance value and a base premium according to
23	the MHPCO price list:
24	
25	- Sword: 1000 G insurance value, 100 G base premium
26	- Amulet: 600 G / 60 G
27	- Staff: 800 G / 80 G
28	- Potion: 400 G / 40 G
29	
30	Components — for example runes and moonstones — are insured at 250 G
31	each, with a base premium of 25 G per component. A building block of
32	3 alike components is offered at a special base premium of 60 G.
33	
34	### Premium modifiers
35	
36	- Cursed items add a 50 % risk surcharge.
37	- Highly enchanted items (enchantment level ≥ 5) add a 30 % risk
38	  surcharge.
39	- Long-standing customers (≥ 2 years of business with MHPCO) receive a
40	  20 % loyalty discount.
41	- A first insurance carries a 10 % initial assessment surcharge.
42	- Customers receive a 15 % discount on each contract after their first.
43	- A 5 G processing fee is added to every premium.
44	
45	All amounts are rounded to whole G in the MHPCO's favor.
46	
47	### Claim processing
48	
49	A deductible of 100 G applies per damage event. The total payout per
50	policy is capped at twice the insurance sum.
51	
52	- Damage to items with enchantment level ≥ 8 is reimbursed at 50 % of
53	  the damage amount.
54	- Damage to items made of dragon material is fully reimbursed.
55	
56	## Examples
57	
58	The examples below illustrate single rules in isolation. Values shown
59	are base premiums or raw payout amounts before integration with other
60	modifiers, unless stated otherwise.
61	
62	### Building block of 3 alike components
63	
64	- 2 runes → 50 G base premium
65	- 3 runes → 60 G base premium (block applies)
66	- 4 runes → 100 G base premium (no block — block requires exactly 3)
67	- 7 runes → 175 G base premium
68	
69	### "Alike" components
70	
71	> ❓ Hmm — "alike" components: does that mean exactly the same type,
72	> or just the same family (rune-y, gemstone-y)?
73	
74	- 2 runes + 1 moonstone → 75 G base premium (no block: different types)
75	- 3 runes + 3 moonstones → 120 G base premium (two separate blocks)
76	
77	### Modifier scope on multi-item policies
78	
79	> ❓ A policy with several items: does the cursed surcharge apply to
80	> the whole policy, or just to the cursed item?
81	
82	- a policy covers a cursed sword (base premium 100 G) and a plain
83	  amulet (base premium 60 G) → policy base premium 160 G; the cursed
84	  surcharge adds 50 G (50 % of the cursed sword's base premium, not
85	  of the policy total) → 210 G before further modifiers and fee
86	- item-specific modifiers (cursed, high enchantment) apply to the
87	  base premium of the affected item; policy-wide modifiers (loyalty,
88	  first insurance, follow-up contract) apply to the policy base
89	  premium (the sum of all item base premiums); the processing fee is
90	  added at the very end
91	
92	### Modifier thresholds
93	
94	- customer with exactly 2 years with MHPCO → loyalty discount applies
95	- sword with exactly enchantment 5 → high-enchantment surcharge
96	  applies; if cursed, both surcharges apply
97	- sword with enchantment 4 → no high-enchantment surcharge; curse
98	  surcharge applies only if cursed
99	- dragon-material sword with exactly enchantment 8, damage 1000 G →
100	  payout 400 G (high-enchantment clause applies, then deductible)
101	
102	### Deductible per damage event
103	
104	- a dragon attack damages an insured sword (500 G) and an insured
105	  amulet (300 G); payout = 600 G (the 100 G deductible applies once
106	  per damaged item)
107	
108	### Standard reimbursement (no special clauses)
109	
110	- regular sword (steel, enchantment 3), damage 500 G → payout 400 G
111	  (full reimbursement minus 100 G deductible; no special clause applies)
112	- damage to a rune (insurance value 250 G), damage 200 G → payout
113	  100 G (full reimbursement minus 100 G deductible; runes have no
114	  enchantment level or material, so no special clause applies)
115	
116	### Enchantment threshold vs. dragon material
117	
118	- dragon-material sword, enchantment 9, damage 1000 G → payout 400 G
119	  (both clauses apply; the 50 % rule wins, then deductible: 500 − 100)
120	- dragon-material sword, enchantment 5, damage 800 G → payout 700 G
121	  (only the dragon-material clause applies: full reimbursement,
122	  then deductible: 800 − 100)
123	- steel sword, enchantment 9, damage 1000 G → payout 400 G
124	  (only the high-enchantment clause applies: 50 % first, then
125	  deductible: 500 − 100)
126	
127	### Multiple items of the same type
128	
129	> ❓ What if a customer brings two of the same item — one in hand,
130	> one in the backpack? Or just two swords because they fight with
131	> two?
132	
133	- a policy covers two swords → insurance sum 2000 G (= 2×1000),
134	  cap 4000 G
135	- a dragon attack damages both swords; `damages` contains two
136	  `{itemType: "sword", ...}` entries → each entry is treated as a
137	  separate damage with its own deductible
138	- if the `damages` array contains more entries of a given type than
139	  the policy actually covers (e.g. two sword damages but only one
140	  sword insured) → the CLI exits with a non-zero status code; the
141	  whole claim is rejected
142	
143	### Cap exhaustion
144	
145	- a policy covers a sword and an amulet → insurance sum 1600 G
146	  (= 1000 + 600, the sum of the items' insurance values), cap 3200 G
147	- a cursed sword (insurance value 1000 G, premium with modifiers
148	  165 G) → cap 2000 G (based on the unmodified insurance value;
149	  premium modifiers do not raise the cap)
150	- a policy covers a sword and 3 runes (a block) → insurance sum
151	  1750 G (= 1000 + 3×250); the block discount affects the premium
152	  only, not the insurance sum
153	- a sword is insured (insurance sum 1000 G, cap 2000 G); two successive
154	  claims of 1500 G each
155	- first claim → payout 1400 G, cap remaining 600 G
156	- second claim → payout 600 G, cap remaining 0 G (the desired 1400 G
157	  is reduced to the remaining cap)
158	
159	### Rounding in the MHPCO's favor
160	
161	- a premium calculation that yields 197.5 G → final premium 198 G
162	  (rounded up)
163	- a payout calculation that yields 350.5 G → final payout 350 G
164	  (rounded down)
165	- intermediate amounts during a calculation are kept as fractions;
166	  only the final premium or payout is rounded
167	
168	### Edge cases
169	
170	- empty item list → premium 5 G (only the processing fee)
171	- quote includes an item with an unknown type (e.g.
172	  `{type: "broomstick"}`) → the CLI exits with a non-zero status code
173	  and writes an error description to stderr; no `results` are written
174	  to stdout
175	- claim references a damage entry whose item is not part of the policy
176	  (e.g. an amulet damaged when only a sword is insured, or an item
177	  with an unknown type) → the CLI exits with a non-zero status code
178	  and writes an error description to stderr
179	- claim contains a damage entry with `amount: -200` → the CLI exits
180	  with a non-zero status code and writes an error description to
181	  stderr
182	
183	## Integration examples
184	
185	The following two examples combine multiple rules to clarify how
186	modifiers stack and how customer history affects the premium.
187	
188	### Newcomer with a cursed sword
189	
190	- customer: 0 years with MHPCO, no previous contract
191	- item: a cursed sword (steel, enchantment 3)
192	- premium: 165 G
193	- (100 G base + 50 G curse + 10 G first insurance = 160 G + 5 G fee = 165 G)
194	
195	### Long-standing customer's second contract
196	
197	> ❓ Wait — does "first insurance" mean the customer's first ever
198	> contract, or the first time we see this particular item? A
199	> long-standing customer with a brand-new sword: does the first
200	> insurance surcharge still apply?
201	
202	- customer: 3 years with MHPCO; this is the customer's second `quote`
203	  in the scenario
204	- item: a cursed sword (steel, enchantment 7)
205	- premium: 160 G
206	- (100 G base + 50 G curse + 30 G high enchantment − 20 G loyalty
207	  + 10 G first insurance − 15 G follow-up contract = 155 G + 5 G fee
208	  = 160 G)
209	- The first insurance surcharge still applies to the new sword, even
210	  though the customer is on a follow-up contract — each item in a
211	  `quote` is treated as a first insurance, regardless of customer
212	  history.
213	
214	## CLI input/output format
215	
216	The implementation must be exposed as a command-line executable
217	`claim-office`. It reads a JSON document from stdin describing a
218	scenario and writes a JSON document with the corresponding results to
219	stdout.
220	
221	A scenario is a JSON object with a `customer` object and a `steps`
222	array. The `customer` describes the single customer for the whole
223	scenario. Each step has an `op` field (`"quote"` or `"claim"`) and the
224	operation-specific input fields. Steps are processed sequentially;
225	later `claim` steps refer to a policy created by an earlier `quote`
226	step via its zero-based step index in a `policy` field.
227	
228	Stdout receives a JSON object with a `results` array of the same length
229	and order as the input `steps`. Each result contains:
230	
231	- For a `quote` step: `premium` (integer, total premium in G).
232	- For a `claim` step: `payout` (integer, payout in G) and
233	  `remainingCap` (integer, cap remaining on the policy after this
234	  claim).
235	
236	### JSON Schema (normative)
237	
238	The field names below are **binding**. Your implementation must use
239	exactly these names; do not rename or restructure them.
240	
241	**Input (stdin):**
242	
243	```json
244	{
245	  "type": "object",
246	  "required": ["customer", "steps"],
247	  "properties": {
248	    "customer": {
249	      "type": "object",
250	      "required": ["yearsWithMHPCO"],
251	      "properties": {
252	        "yearsWithMHPCO": { "type": "integer" }
253	      }
254	    },
255	    "steps": {
256	      "type": "array",
257	      "items": {
258	        "oneOf": [
259	          {
260	            "description": "Quote step",
261	            "required": ["op", "items"],
262	            "properties": {
263	              "op": { "const": "quote" },
264	              "items": {
265	                "type": "array",
266	                "items": {
267	                  "type": "object",
268	                  "required": ["type"],
269	                  "properties": {
270	                    "type":        { "type": "string", "description": "sword | amulet | staff | potion | rune | moonstone" },
271	                    "material":    { "type": "string" },
272	                    "enchantment": { "type": "integer" },
273	                    "cursed":      { "type": "boolean" }
274	                  }
275	                }
276	              }
277	            }
278	          },
279	          {
280	            "description": "Claim step",
281	            "required": ["op", "policy", "incident"],
282	            "properties": {
283	              "op":     { "const": "claim" },
284	              "policy": { "type": "integer", "description": "zero-based index of the quote step that created the policy" },
285	              "incident": {
286	                "type": "object",
287	                "required": ["cause", "damages"],
288	                "properties": {
289	                  "cause": { "type": "string" },
290	                  "damages": {
291	                    "type": "array",
292	                    "items": {
293	                      "type": "object",
294	                      "required": ["itemType", "amount"],
295	                      "properties": {
296	                        "itemType": { "type": "string" },
297	                        "amount":   { "type": "integer" }
298	                      }
299	                    }
300	                  }
301	                }
302	              }
303	            }
304	          }
305	        ]
306	      }
307	    }
308	  }
309	}
310	```

316	  "type": "object",
317	  "required": ["results"],
318	  "properties": {
319	    "results": {
320	      "type": "array",
321	      "items": {

351	  "customer": {"yearsWithMHPCO": 5},

# Predictive Test-Driven Development

Use TDD as an empirical feedback loop: predict, check, compare, and let the evidence determine the next change.

## Context: 

## Core rules

The prediction requirement applies only within the TDD workflow. Routine repository, file, and administrative operations do not require predictions.

1. Work on exactly one observable behavior at a time.
2. Before every deterministic check, state a concrete, falsifiable prediction and run the check immediately.
3. Compare predicted and actual outcomes explicitly. Never rewrite an unexpected result as predicted.
4. A valid Red fails because the active behavior is missing, for the predicted reason.
5. Investigate prediction mismatches before changing production behavior.
6. Implement only enough to satisfy the active behavior and keep previous behavior green.
7. Refactor only while behavior tests are green.
8. Do not invent unspecified behavior; resolve ambiguous observable contracts by stating the reading you adopt.

## Preparation

Before the first cycle:

1. Read the complete specification and identify every rule, example, boundary, and ambiguity.
2. Create or review an ordered test list. Keep future tests inactive.
3. Determine the project's stack and commands. If `stacks/` contains a matching profile, read it before changing code.
4. Establish a baseline with the applicable behavior, compilation/type, lint, and smell checks. Predict each check before running it.

## One predictive cycle

### 1. Activate one behavior

State its given/input, operation, and exact expected outcome in domain language. Choose the smallest public observation that proves it, then activate or write exactly one test.

### 2. Reach behavioral Red

Open the phase with the `## Red` marker (see "Mandatory output markers" below), then inspect the current code and predict the narrowest test's load/compile/execution outcome, failure category, and relevant message or values. Run it and compare.

If loading or compilation prevents the assertion from running, add only enough scaffold to reach the behavioral failure. Predict and check again. Do not implement the behavior until Red fails for the intended reason.

If the new test already passes, confirm that prediction, record that no production change was needed, and do not manufacture a failure.

Close the phase with the `Red Phase Complete:` block and both prediction lines.

### 3. Reach Green minimally

Open the phase with the `## Green` marker. Make the smallest production change likely to pass the active test without anticipating inactive examples. Hardcoded values and narrow conditionals are valid intermediate steps.

Predict and run the focused test. Include expected pass/fail and todo counts when available. Compare the result; investigate any mismatch before continuing.

### 4. Inspect and refactor

While green, review the code against the Four Rules of Simple Design, in order:

1. Passes the tests
2. Reveals intention
3. Contains no duplication, including duplicated knowledge
4. Has the fewest elements

Use domain-appropriate names and do not leak temporary implementation details into them. Linters and smell detectors are evidence, not substitutes for this review.

Make at most one refactoring at a time. Predict and run the smallest relevant check after each. If no refactoring improves the Four Rules, leave the code unchanged.

**In this workflow the refactoring runs in this context.** Open the phase with
the `## Refactor` marker (see below) and emit it also when the review concludes
that no refactoring improves the code.

### 5. Close once

Predict and run the complete suite and all other applicable gates from the stack profile. Do not run the complete suite both before and during this closing step unless investigating a mismatch.

Close with a compact record of the behavior, Red evidence, minimal Green change or already-green result, refactoring decision, final gates, and next inactive behavior. Then start the next cycle immediately.

## Mandatory output markers

Predictions and phases are read mechanically from your output text. Emit these markers verbatim.

| Phase     | Marker                                            |
|-----------|---------------------------------------------------|
| Test List | `## Test List` + `Test List Created:`             |
| Red       | `## Red` heading                                  |
| Red       | `Red Phase Complete:` plus both prediction lines  |
| Green     | `## Green` heading                                |
| Refactor  | `## Refactor` heading                             |

Red phase output:

```
## Red -- Test N: <test description>

<prediction and failure verification steps>

Red Phase Complete:
**Compilation Prediction**: <what you expected> ✅ Correct
**Runtime Prediction**: <what you expected> ✅ Correct

<result summary>
```

Emit **both** prediction lines, verbatim, each ending in `✅ Correct` or `❌ Incorrect`. Do not abbreviate them, do not summarize them as "both correct", and do not collapse them into one line. This is the mechanical form of Core rule 3: an unexpected result is recorded as `Incorrect` and investigated, never rewritten as predicted.

When the activated test already passes, write:

```
## Red -- Test N: <test description>

Test already passes -- no new failure to fix. No production change needed.
```

Green phase output:

```
## Green -- <brief summary of what was added>
```

Refactor phase output:

```
## Refactor -- <brief summary of what was improved, or "no improvement possible">
```

This heading is the only signal that the Four Rules review happened. Emit it
every cycle, including the cycles where the review changes nothing.

## Prediction mismatch

When actual and predicted outcomes differ:

1. State that the prediction was incorrect and preserve both outcomes.
2. Stop feature implementation.
3. Use the smallest deterministic check to explain whether the cause is existing behavior, test setup, command/environment, load/compile failure, quality tooling, coupling, or regression.
4. Make a new evidence-based prediction and check it.
5. Resume only after the discrepancy is understood.

Never change production behavior merely to make an unexplained failure disappear.

## Completion

A feature is complete only when every specified example has an executable test, all behavior tests and applicable quality gates pass, mismatches are explained, the Four Rules review is complete, and no unagreed behavior was added.

# TDD Test List Phase

You are now in the **Test List Phase** of TDD. Follow these instructions to create a comprehensive test list.

## Your Mission

Create a test list using `it.todo()` that covers **every rule and every example** from the specification:
1. Read the specification (`prompt.md`) thoroughly -- every rule, every example, every clarifying question (?)
2. Turn each example into at least one `it.todo()` test case
3. Order tests from simplest to most complex
4. Use `it.todo()` only -- NO executable tests yet

## Context: 

## Process

### Step 1: Understand the Feature
Read the complete specification. Pay special attention to integration examples and clarifying
questions (marked with ?) -- these disambiguate rules that may seem open to interpretation in isolation.
- What are all the operations the system must support?
- What rules govern each operation?
- Which examples in the spec illustrate these rules?
- For rejection or failure cases, what is the observable error contract: a thrown error, an error result, a status, or another outcome? If an error is thrown, does the specification define its type and/or message?

### Step 2: Identify Test Cases from the Spec
Walk through the specification section by section. For each rule and each example:
- Create a test case that verifies the described behavior
- Include the **expected values from the spec** in the test description
- If a clarifying question (?) resolves an ambiguity, create a test for the clarified interpretation
- If the spec uses an example-mapping format (rules, examples, questions), every listed example must have a corresponding test
- Make every rejection or failure case explicit in observable terms, such as `throws RangeError`, `returns an error result`, or `responds with status 400`
- Include an exact error type or message only when the specification establishes it
- If the specification merely says `rejects`, `fails`, `invalid`, or equivalent without defining the observable contract, choose the most defensible reading of the specification, state that reading explicitly in the test description, and continue; do not silently invent an unstated contract

### Step 3: Order Tests (Simple -> Complex)
Arrange tests in increasing complexity:
1. Simplest case (often empty/zero/single item)
2. Individual rules in isolation
3. Rules with modifiers
4. Combinations of multiple rules
5. Multi-step scenarios (e.g., operations that reference earlier results)

### Step 4: Write Test File
Create the test file with `it.todo()` entries:

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { functionName } from "./implementation.js";

describe("Feature Name", () => {
  it.todo("should [behavior] -- [expected value from spec]");
  it.todo("throws RangeError when [invalid condition from spec]");
  it.todo("should [next behavior] -- [expected value from spec]");
  // ... ordered simple -> complex, covering ALL spec examples
});
```

### Step 5: Provide Summary

After creating the test list, output both marker lines followed by the summary.
The heading and the `Test List Created` line are read by different parsers --
emit both, verbatim:

```
## Test List

Test List Created:
**Feature**: [feature name]
**Test File**: [filename].spec.ts
**Tests**: [count]

**Test Cases** (ordered simple -> complex):
1. [first test description]
2. [second test description]
3. [third test description]
...
```

Do not treat this summary as the end of your turn -- it is a checkpoint
inside one continuous run. Proceed straight into the Red phase.

## Important Guidelines

### DO
- Cover **every spec example** with at least one test
- Cover **every operation** described in the spec
- Give **every clarifying question (?)** a corresponding test
- Order tests **simple -> complex**
- Use `it.todo()` for all tests
- Include **expected values** in descriptions
- State rejection and failure outcomes as explicit observable contracts
- Name your chosen reading explicitly when the spec leaves a failure mechanism open
- Keep tests **independent**
- One behavior per test

### DON'T
- Write executable tests (use `it.todo()`)
- Think about implementation instead of behavior
- Turn vague words such as `rejects` into an invented error contract without saying so
- Leave a rejection test vague when its observable outcome is known
- Miss an entire operation described in the spec
- Order randomly

Let me analyze the spec carefully to design the domain. Key architecture: I'll create a domain module (`claimOffice.ts`) with `quote` and `claim` (or a scenario processor `runScenario`), plus `cli.ts`. Given the sequential scenario processing with stateful cap and customer history, I'll build a scenario runner. But for TDD I'll start with the smallest units: premium calculation.

Let me think about the domain modeling before writing the test list:

**Quote/Premium calculation:**
- Item base premiums: sword 100, amulet 60, staff 80, potion 40, component (rune/moonstone) 25.
- Component blocks: exactly 3 alike (same type) → 60 instead of 75.
- Item-specific modifiers on item base premium: cursed +50%, high enchantment (≥5) +30%.
- Policy-wide modifiers on policy base premium (sum of item base premiums): loyalty (≥2 yrs) −20%, first insurance +10%, follow-up contract −15% (after first quote).
- Wait — first insurance surcharge: "each item in a quote is treated as a first insurance". Let me re-read.

The integration example: cursed sword steel ench 7, 3 yrs, second quote: 100 base + 50 curse + 30 high ench − 20 loyalty + 10 first insurance − 15 follow-up = 155 + 5 fee = 160.

So: item base = 100. Item modifiers: curse 50% of 100 = 50, high ench 30% of 100 = 30. Policy base = sum of item bases = 100. Loyalty −20% of policy base = −20. First insurance +10% of policy base = +10. Follow-up −15% of policy base = −15. Then +5 fee.

So all policy-wide percentages apply to the policy base premium (sum of item base premiums, NOT including item surcharges). Let me verify with newcomer: cursed sword ench 3, 0 yrs, first contract: 100 + 50 curse + 10 first insurance = 160 + 5 = 165. ✓ (no high ench since 3<5, no loyalty since 0<2, no follow-up since first).

First insurance: "each item in a quote is treated as a first insurance, regardless of customer history." So the first-insurance surcharge is 10% per... item? Let me re-read. The 10% initial assessment surcharge. In the example there's one item. Given "each item is treated as a first insurance", the surcharge is 10% of each item's base premium. With one item = 10% of 100 = 10. So first-insurance = 10% of policy base (sum of item bases) always applies. That matches.

Follow-up contract −15%: "Customers receive a 15% discount on each contract after their first." This is per-quote-step in the scenario. First quote step: no follow-up discount. Second+ quote step: −15% of policy base.

So I need scenario-level state: count of quotes done so far (to know if follow-up), and cap tracking per policy.

Let me define ordering of operations. Formula:
```
itemBase = priceListBase(item) [with block discount for components]
itemSurcharge = itemBase * (cursed?0.5:0) + itemBase * (ench>=5?0.3:0)
policyBase = sum(itemBase)
policyAdjust = policyBase * (loyalty?-0.2:0) + policyBase*0.1 (first insurance always) + policyBase*(followup?-0.15:0)
premium = policyBase + sum(itemSurcharge) + policyAdjust + 5
round up (favor MHPCO)
```

Wait, but blocks: components. Block of exactly 3 alike → 60. Let me handle component base premium by grouping same type components: for each group of same type, count n; blocks = floor(n/3) each 60, remainder each 25. Verify: 3 runes → 60 ✓. 4 runes → one block (60) + 1 (25) = 85? But spec says 4 runes → 100 (no block). 

Re-read: "4 runes → 100 G base premium (no block — block requires exactly 3)". So block only applies when the count is EXACTLY 3, not floor division. 7 runes → 175 (=7×25, no block). So: if group count == exactly 3 → 60, else n×25. Let me verify: 3 runes + 3 moonstones → 120 (two separate blocks, 60+60) ✓. 2 runes + 1 moonstone → 75 (25×2 + 25×1, no block since neither type has 3) ✓. 2 runes → 50 ✓.

So block rule: per component-type group, if exactly 3 → 60, otherwise count × 25.

**Claim processing:**
- Policy has insurance sum = sum of item insurance values (unmodified). Cap = 2 × insurance sum.
- Per damage event (each damage entry): deductible 100 G.
- Item ench ≥8 → 50% of damage. Dragon material → full. If both: 50% rule wins (dragon+high ench → 50%). Then deductible.
- Order: apply clause (50% or full) to damage amount, then subtract deductible (100), floor at 0? Then cap.
- Cap: total payout per policy capped at 2× insurance sum, across successive claims (stateful remaining cap).
- Rounding payout: down (favor MHPCO).

Let me verify examples:
- dragon sword ench 8, dmg 1000 → 50% (ench≥8 wins) = 500, − 100 = 400. ✓
- dragon sword ench 9, dmg 1000 → 500 − 100 = 400 ✓
- dragon sword ench 5, dmg 800 → dragon full = 800, −100 = 700 ✓
- steel sword ench 9, dmg 1000 → 500 −100 = 400 ✓
- regular sword ench 3 dmg 500 → 500 − 100 = 400 ✓
- rune dmg 200 → 200 −100 = 100 ✓
- dragon attack 2 items sword 500 amulet 300 → (500−100)+(300−100) = 400+200 = 600 ✓ (deductible per item)

Cap exhaustion: sword insurance sum 1000, cap 2000. Two claims of 1500 each:
- first: 1500 − 100 = 1400, within remaining cap 2000 → payout 1400, remaining 600.
- second: 1500 − 100 = 1400, but remaining cap 600 → payout 600, remaining 0. ✓

So payout per claim = min(sum of damage-item computations, remaining cap). Remaining cap decreases.

Deductible per damage: is deductible applied before clause or after? "Damage to items with ench≥8 reimbursed at 50% of damage amount" then deductible. dragon ench 8 dmg 1000: 50% = 500, then deductible 100 → 400. So clause first, then deductible. Floor at 0 if negative (deductible larger than reimbursement)? Not specified but defensible — floor at 0.

Error cases (CLI exits non-zero, writes to stderr):
- Unknown item type in quote.
- Claim references item not in policy (wrong type, or more damages of a type than covered, or unknown type).
- Damage amount negative.

"Multiple items of the same type": damages array with more entries of a type than policy covers → reject whole claim. So I need to count coverage per type and match damages against available items (each damage consumes one covered item of that type). Also each damage needs to know the item's enchantment/material — from the policy's items. Which item does a damage entry map to? Damage entry has only itemType and amount. So it maps to an insured item of that type. If multiple of same type, which one's enchantment applies? The spec's two-swords example uses a dragon attack on both. I'll match damages to insured items of the same type in order; each damage consumes one item. The item's stored properties (material, enchantment) determine the clause.

Now let me write the test list. I'll structure the code as `claimOffice.ts` exposing a `runScenario(input)` function returning `{results}`, plus helper functions I can test in isolation. But the cleanest TDD path is to test the public behaviors. Given the spec examples are mostly about premium and payout numbers, I'll test through `runScenario` for integration but that requires full plumbing early. 

Better: build up with smaller pure functions `premium(...)` and `payout(...)` first, then the scenario runner and CLI. However the spec's binding contract is the CLI/scenario JSON. To keep tests aligned with spec examples while allowing incremental TDD, I'll expose:
- `quotePremium(customer, items, context)` 
- and a scenario runner `runScenario`.

Actually, to keep it clean and spec-driven, I'll drive everything through `runScenario` since customer history/follow-up/cap are scenario-stateful. But early tests (base premium of a sword) are easier as unit calls. Let me use a hybrid: a `computePremium` function that takes explicit flags (isFollowUp) and the customer, and `computeClaim`. Then a thin `runScenario` orchestrates. I'll test `computePremium`/`computeClaim` directly for the isolated examples and `runScenario` for multi-step ones.
